The Gutenberg Bible is the first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type, produced by Johannes Gutenberg and his partners in Mainz, Germany, and finished by about 1455. It marks the start of the age of printed books in the West.

It is the Latin Bible used by the Church, the Vulgate, in two large volumes, with 42 lines to a column. That is why it is also called the 42-line Bible. Some copies were printed on paper, some on vellum, and each was bought unbound and then decorated by hand, so no two are quite alike.

What Gutenberg put together:

  • Metal letters cast in a hand mould, so that many identical copies of each letter could be made.
  • An oil based ink that stuck to metal.
  • A screw press adapted from presses used for wine and paper.

Copies were on sale by 1455; a future pope saw pages at Frankfurt that year and praised how readable they were. Perhaps 180 copies were made, and around 49 survive, whole or in part. Gutenberg himself lost the business to his financier, Johann Fust.

Printing spread fast: by 1500 there were presses in over 200 European towns. Books got cheaper and more numerous, texts became fixed and identical, and ideas moved faster than censors. Within two generations, print carried Martin Luther's pamphlets across Germany and made the Reformation possible. Movable type had been used earlier in China and Korea, but there it had a smaller effect.
